draft.title: Summary and indictable offences
card: a minor offence, such as offensive language or a minor traffic offence. It is heard by a magistrate in the Magistrates' Court, with no jury.
a serious offence, such as murder, armed robbery or large-scale drug supply. It can be tried by a judge and jury in a higher court, such as the County Court or the Supreme Court.
Many indictable offences start in the Magistrates' Court, where a magistrate handles early steps. The most serious ones then go to a higher court for trial.
The type of offence depends on how serious the law treats it. It does not depend on how the accused pleads or how long the case takes.
draft.remember: Minor offences go to a magistrate. Serious offences can go to a judge and jury.

a.q: Which feature is normally true of a summary offence in Victoria?
opts: It is heard by a magistrate without a jury
It is tried by a judge and jury
It is heard in the Supreme Court
It is decided by the police, not a court
a.why: Summary offences are minor and are heard by a magistrate alone. A jury is linked to indictable offences, so the second option is the tempting mistake.
a.clue: Think about who hears minor matters and whether a jury is used.

b.q: Dev is charged with armed robbery. His first court appearance is in the Magistrates' Court. How is his offence best classed, and why?
opts: Indictable, because it is serious and can go before a jury
Summary, because it first appears in the Magistrates' Court
Summary, because Dev may plead guilty to the charge
Indictable, because a magistrate hears it without a jury
b.why: The law treats armed robbery as serious, so it is indictable and can be tried by a judge and jury. Appearing first in the Magistrates' Court does not make an offence summary, because many indictable offences begin there.
b.clue: Where a case first appears may not tell you its type.

a.best: It is heard by a magistrate without a jury

b.best: Indictable, because it is serious and can go before a jury
